title: Only One judges alone (Avot 4:8)
hookLine: a director alone at midnight with the cast list: don't judge alone, for only One judges alone
tomorrow: the money's gone. does the practice go with it?

cards: A kitchen table after midnight. A stack of audition photos, a laptop open to a blank cast list, cold tea. The student director watched every audition herself.
Nobody else was in the room. The list goes up after school tomorrow, and every name on it is her call. She types the last name, hovers over send, and stops.
Something about doing this alone sits wrong, and she can't say what. A sage in Pirkei Avot can.

teach.b: Rabbi Ishmael, son of Rabbi Yose, says it in two short lines. Don't judge alone, for none judges alone but One. And don't say, accept my view, for they may say that, and not you.

teach.h: ONLY GOD SEES THE WHOLE CASE.
teach.b: In this saying, judging by yourself belongs to God alone, because only God sees the whole case: the motive, the history, the part nobody said out loud. Every human judge sees a slice.
So the Mishnah builds courts out of more than one person.

teach.h: EVEN A LOAN GETS THREE JUDGES.
teach.b: Elsewhere it sets three judges even for a quarrel over money. Here's the one to tell a friend tonight: in the Mishnah, a dispute about a loan doesn't get one judge. It gets three.
Don't say, accept my view. Your colleagues, as a group, may say that to you.
You, alone, may not say it to them. Even when you're right, rightness doesn't hand you the gavel. That's the answer to the midnight table.
The director has the authority. But a cast list is a verdict about people, and this saying treats every verdict as too big for one pair of eyes. So she texts the stage manager a photo of the list.
Two minutes later: are you sure about the second lead? She wasn't, it turns out.

how: Jewish courts (a beit din) sit as a panel rather than a single judge, and in study many Jews learn in pairs, a chavruta, so no reading of a text goes unchallenged.

games.q: what does “only one judges alone” mean?
o: a judge should decide alone to keep the case pure
God alone may judge by himself; people judge together
only one person in a family may settle a quarrel

games.q: the saying, piece by piece — tap the pairs.
p: son of Rabbi Yose, says don't judge alone
God alone sees the whole case
the group may say it; one person may not

s: the saying means good judges never need advice
it says the opposite: none judges alone but One, so people judge together.
even when you're right, you may not tell your colleagues to accept your view
they may say it, as a group; you, alone, may not.
in the Mishnah, a dispute over a loan is heard by three judges
the Mishnah sets three judges even for a quarrel over money.

games.q: you're grading your study group's shared project, and you're sure one member slacked. the group report is due tonight. what does Rabbi Ishmael's line point to?
o: show your notes to one other member and ask what they saw before writing it up.
write it up yourself; you were there, you saw it, and you're right.
leave it out entirely, since judging anyone is God's job alone.
games.why: the saying doesn't ban judging; courts judge. it bans judging alone. a second pair of eyes is the default, not a weakness.

practice: Take a pen and paper. Write one call you've been making alone this week, a verdict about a person, a plan, a choice, in a single line.
Under it, write the name of one person who'd see the part you can't, and rest your eyes on the two lines for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Only One judges alone. Rabbi Ishmael's line: judging by yourself belongs to God, so people judge together.

orig.note: Hebrew: don't be a judge alone. yechidi, alone, is the word the saying turns on.

carryVoice: Keep this one: only one judges alone, and it isn't you or me. Thirty days into the rest of Avot.

sources.ref: Mishnah Avot 4:8 (Rabbi Ishmael son of Rabbi Yose: don't judge alone; don't say accept my view)
Mishnah Avot 4:6 (Rabbi Yose: whoever honors the Torah is honored)
